title: Chapter 58: Management of the Poisoned Patient
source: Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 16th Edition, Chapter 58 (Craig Smollin; Stephen Petrou)
file: Katzung Chapter 58_ Management of the Poisoned Patient.pdf
lecture: 10/13 (Toxic Responses) and 10/14 (Treating Poisonings); the treating-poisonings lecture continues 10/19
about: The chapter reviews the basic principles of poisoning, initial management, and specialized treatment of poisoning, including methods of increasing the elimination of drugs and toxins. It defines toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics and describes how volume of distribution, clearance, first-pass metabolism, protein binding and first-order versus zero-order elimination change in overdose, and how therapeutic index and the shape of the dose-response curve determine the severity of an intoxication. It describes how poisoned patients die, the ABCD supportive measures, the toxicologically oriented history and physical examination, laboratory and imaging procedures (anion gap, osmol gap, electrocardiogram) and the limits of toxicology screening. It then covers skin and gastrointestinal decontamination (gastric lavage, activated charcoal, cathartics and whole bowel irrigation), specific antidotes (Table 58-3) and methods of enhancing elimination (dialysis, urinary pH manipulation). A final section describes common toxic syndromes, from acetaminophen to theophylline, with the clinical features and treatment of each.

read_for: Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics - Volume of Distribution: why a large Vd (>5 L/kg) defeats hemodialysis, and the lists of large-Vd drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol, verapamil) and small-Vd drugs (<1 L/kg: salicylate, acetaminophen, ethanol, phenobarbital, lithium, valproic acid, phenytoin).

Special Aspects of Toxicokinetics - Clearance: the paragraph listing how overdose alters kinetics (slowed dissolution or gastric emptying, GI epithelial injury increasing absorption, reduced first-pass effect, exceeded protein-binding capacity, first-order elimination becoming zero-order with a prolonged half-life) - every deck bullet on that slide comes from it.

Special Aspects of Toxicodynamics: therapeutic index versus overlap of therapeutic and toxic curves, drug A (linear) versus drug B (plateau), the tricyclic sweating/seizure hyperpyrexia example and the beta blocker/calcium channel blocker effect on renal and hepatic elimination.

Decontamination - B. Gastrointestinal Tract: emesis no longer recommended; gastric lavage technique and airway requirement; activated charcoal 10:1 ratio and the poisons it does not bind; repeated-dose charcoal 'gut dialysis'; whole bowel irrigation with GoLYTELY/CoLyte at 1-2 L/h until the rectal effluent is clear.
Table 58-2 Hemodialysis in drug overdose and poisoning: the drugs for which hemodialysis may be indicated and those for which it is not useful (the Vd principle in practice).
Methods of Enhancing Elimination of Toxins - A. Dialysis Procedures: why efficiency depends on molecular weight, water solubility, protein binding, endogenous clearance and distribution.

Beta Blockers and Calcium Channel Blockers sections: the two classes whose evidence-based out-of-hospital guideline abstracts she assigned (glucagon for beta blockers; whole bowel irrigation and charcoal for sustained-release calcium antagonists, calcium, high-dose insulin).
Case Study and Case Study Answer: activated charcoal slurry by nasogastric tube as the example of preventing absorption.

terms.chapter_definition: the absorption, distribution, excretion, and metabolism of toxins, toxic doses of therapeutic agents, and their metabolites.
the injurious effects of these substances on body functions.

the apparent volume into which a substance is distributed in the body; a mathematical representation that describes, inversely, how much of the drug remains in the vascular system. A large Vd implies the drug distributes from the blood to other tissues and is not readily accessible to measures aimed at purifying the blood, such as hemodialysis.
a measure of the volume of plasma that is cleared of drug per unit time; the total clearance for most drugs is the sum of clearances via excretion by the kidneys and metabolism by the liver.
If the capacity of the liver to metabolize a drug is exceeded, the first-pass effect will be reduced and more drug will be delivered to the circulation.
At normal dosage, most drugs are eliminated at a rate proportional to the plasma concentration.

If the plasma concentration is very high and normal metabolism is saturated, the rate of elimination may become fixed; this change may markedly prolong the apparent serum half-life and increase toxicity.

Both the therapeutic index and the overlap of therapeutic and toxic response curves must be considered; two drugs may have the same therapeutic index but unequal safe dosing ranges if the slopes of their dose-response curves are not the same.
removing toxins from the skin or gastrointestinal tract, undertaken simultaneously with initial stabilization, diagnostic assessment, and laboratory evaluation.

performed, if the patient is awake or the airway is protected by an endotracheal tube, using an orogastric or nasogastric tube as large as possible; lavage solutions (usually 0.9% saline) should be at body temperature.

owing to its large surface area, can adsorb many drugs and poisons; most effective if given in a ratio of at least 10:1 of charcoal to estimated dose of toxin by weight; does not bind iron, lithium, or potassium, and binds alcohols and cyanide only poorly.

repeated doses of oral activated charcoal may enhance systemic elimination of some drugs (including carbamazepine, dapsone, and phenobarbital) by a mechanism referred to as 'gut dialysis', although the clinical benefit is unproved.

a balanced polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution (GoLYTELY, CoLyte) given orally at 1-2 L/h (500 mL/h in children) for several hours until the rectal effluent is clear; enhances gut decontamination after ingestion of iron tablets, enteric-coated medicines, illicit drug-filled packets, and foreign bodies.

more efficient than peritoneal dialysis; its efficiency is a function of the molecular weight, water solubility, protein binding, endogenous clearance, and distribution in the body of the specific toxin.

listen: This reading is Chapter 58, Management of the Poisoned Patient, by Craig Smollin and Stephen Petrou, in Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology, sixteenth edition. It was not discussed in class as a reading. Its toxicokinetics section matches her slides, and it is the source of her table's tricyclic and salicylate rows. In overdose, a drug with a large volume of distribution sits in the tissues, so hemodialysis removes it poorly and must run a long time. Saturated liver metabolism reduces the first pass effect, so more drug circulates. A poison can injure the gut and increase absorption. Tricyclic antidepressants: tachycardia, dilated pupils, dry mouth, agitation, seizures, sometimes vasodilation, an elongated Q R S interval, and reduced cardiac contractility. Treatment is intravenous fluids, dopamine or norepinephrine, and sodium bicarbonate for the elongated Q R S. Bicarbonate counteracts the inhibition of cardiac sodium channels. Salicylates: hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, then metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia, confusion and seizures. Treatment is supportive care and intravenous sodium bicarbonate, which traps the salicylate in the urine as a negatively charged ion and enhances its elimination. The trap. Bicarbonate does two different jobs. In tricyclic overdose it counteracts sodium channel block. In salicylate overdose it traps the drug in the urine.
